1.description: This slide introduces the concepts of convex sets and convex combinations in the context of convex analysis, specifically chapter 10 of a textbook by LVJ.  Definition 1 states that a set $S$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$ is convex if, for any two points $z_1$ and $z_2$ in $S$, the line segment connecting them (represented by the convex combination $tz_1 + (1-t)z_2$ where $0 \le t \le 1$) is entirely contained within $S$.  A simple illustration shows two points $z_1$ and $z_2$ and the line segment between them. Definition 2 defines a convex combination of $n$ points $z_1, z_2, \dots, z_n$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$ as a weighted sum $t_1 z_1 + t_2 z_2 + \dots + t_n z_n$, where the weights $t_i$ are non-negative and sum to 1.  The illustrations show examples of convex combinations for two and three points, forming a line segment and a triangle respectively.  The context of linear programming is relevant because convexity is a crucial property of feasible regions in linear programming problems.

figures.description: Theorem 10.1 statement and proof outline.

2.description: This slide presents Theorem 10.1, which states that a set $S$ is convex if and only if it contains all convex combinations of its points. The proof focuses on one direction of the implication: if $S$ contains all convex combinations of its points, then $S$ is convex.  The proof begins by assuming that $S$ contains all convex combinations of its points. Then, it shows that for any two points $z_1$ and $z_2$ in $S$, their convex combination $tz_1 + (1-t)z_2$ (where $0 \le t \le 1$) is also in $S$ by the assumption. This directly satisfies the definition of a convex set, thus proving that $S$ is convex. The underlining highlights the key assumption and conclusion of this part of the proof. The notation "pf" indicates "proof," and the double-headed arrow indicates the "if and only if" nature of the theorem. "conv. comb." is an abbreviation for "convex combination". The context of linear programming is crucial because this theorem is fundamental to understanding the properties of feasible regions in linear programming problems, which are often convex sets.

Since the inner convex combination is in $S$ (by the base case), and the outer convex combination is also in $S$ (by the definition of convexity), the entire expression is in $S$. 8.description: This slide presents Caratheodory's Theorem (Theorem 10.3) and outlines the beginning of its proof within the context of linear programming. The theorem states that the convex hull of a set $S$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$, denoted conv($S$), consists of all convex combinations of $m+1$ points from $S$.  The proof begins by restating the definition of the convex hull as the set of all convex combinations of points from $S$, but with the key difference that it uses only $n$ points instead of $m+1$.  The proof then introduces a linear program (LP) to find a convex combination of points in $S$ that equals a given point $z$. The LP maximizes $c^T x$ subject to $Ax = z$, where $A$ is a matrix whose columns are points from $S$, and $x$ is a vector of coefficients representing the convex combination. The constraint $\sum x_i = 1$ ensures that the combination is convex, and $x_i \ge 0$ ensures non-negativity of the coefficients.  The underlining highlights the theorem statement and the key equation in the proof. The notation "conv(S)" represents the convex hull of set $S$, and the subscript $m \times n$ indicates the dimensions of matrix $A$. The context of linear programming is crucial because the proof uses an LP to demonstrate the theorem.  The theorem itself is important because it provides a bound on the number of points needed to represent any point in the convex hull, which has implications for computational efficiency in linear programming algorithms.

LEMMA 10.5. The system $Ax \le b$ has no solutions if and only if there is a $y$ such that
$$
\begin{aligned}
A^Ty &= 0 \\
y &\ge 0 \\
b^Ty &< 0
\end{aligned}
$$
(10.8) \\
PROOF. Consider the linear program
\begin{align*} \label{eq:1}
\text{maximize } & 0 \\
\text{subject to } & Ax \le b
\end{align*} 
and its dual
\begin{align*}
\text{minimize } & b^Ty \\
\text{subject to } & A^Ty = 0 \\
& y \ge 0
\end{align*}

15.description: This slide presents Farkas' Lemma (Lemma 10.5), a fundamental result in linear programming. The lemma states that the system of inequalities $Ax \le b$ has no solution if and only if there exists a vector $y$ satisfying the conditions $A^Ty = 0$, $y \ge 0$, and $b^Ty < 0$. The proof outline begins by considering a primal linear program that maximizes 0 subject to $Ax \le b$.  The dual of this linear program is then introduced, which minimizes $b^Ty$ subject to $A^Ty = 0$ and $y \ge 0$. The proof likely proceeds by showing the equivalence between the primal problem having no feasible solution and the dual problem being unbounded (or having an objective function value less than 0). This connection between the primal and dual problems is a key element of linear programming duality theory. The equation number (10.8) suggests this is equation 10.8 in the textbook or lecture notes. The context of linear programming is crucial because Farkas' Lemma is a cornerstone of the theory, used extensively in proving other important results, such as the strong duality theorem and the separation theorem.

in the variables $x_1, \dots, x_n$. Then the objective function $f(x) := x^T Q^T Q x - \sum_{j=1}^n x_j P_j^T P_j$ is convex, and the following statements hold.

(ii) There exists a point $p^*$ such that $p^* = Qx^*$ holds for every optimal solution $x^*$. Moreover, the ball with center $p^*$ and squared radius $-f(x^*)$ is the unique ball of smallest radius containing $P$.

1.description: This slide discusses the efficiency of the simplex method in linear programming.  It contrasts the worst-case and average-case performance.  The worst-case scenario, attributed to Dantzig, is characterized by problem dimensions where $m < 50$ and $m + n < 200$, where $m$ is the number of constraints and $n$ is the number of variables.  The average number of iterations required is typically bounded above by $\frac{3m}{2}$, although in rare cases, it might approach $3m$.  Two tables (Table 4.1 and Table 4.2) present empirical data on the average number of iterations needed for different problem sizes ($m$ and $n$) using two different pivot rules: the largest-coefficient rule and the largest-increase rule. The context of the course (Linear Programming) is crucial for understanding the practical implications of these efficiency considerations when choosing a solution method for linear programming problems.

\textbf{Other Pivoting Rules (independent of scale)} \\
$[LMG]$ largest increase, steepest edge, Bland Rule ... \\
\textbf{ALTERNATIVE PIVOTING RULES} \\
Thus we are led to ranking the candidates $x_j$ for entering the basis according to \\
criteria that are independent of changes of scale. One criterion of this kind is the in- \\
crease in the objective function obtained when $x_j$ actually enters the basis. The \\
resulting rule (always choose that candidate whose entrance into the basis brings \\
about the largest increase in the objective function) is referred to as the \textit{largest-} \\
\textit{increase rule}. On the Klee-Minty examples (4.2), the largest-increase rule leads the \\
simplex method to the optimal solution in only one iteration, as opposed to the \\
$2^n - 1$ iterations required by the previously used largest-coefficient rule. However, \\
the new rule does not always lead to a small number of iterations: R. G. Jeroslow \\
(1973) constructed LP problems that are to the largest-increase rule what the Klee- \\
Minty problems are to the largest-coefficient rule. (More precisely, the number of \\
iterations required by the largest-increase rule grows exponentially with $m$ and $n$.) \\
Again, these examples exploit the myopia inherent in the simplex method. It is \\
conceivable that every easily implemented rule for choosing the entering variable \\
can be tricked in a similar way into requiring very large numbers of iterations.

6.description: This slide discusses alternative pivoting rules in the simplex method for linear programming, focusing on rules independent of scale.  It introduces the "largest-increase rule," which selects the entering variable that maximizes the increase in the objective function. The slide contrasts this rule with the largest-coefficient rule, highlighting that while the largest-increase rule solves the Klee-Minty problem (4.2) in only one iteration (compared to the exponentially many iterations required by the largest-coefficient rule), it is not immune to worst-case exponential behavior.  The work of R.G. Jeroslow (1973) is cited, showing that the largest-increase rule also suffers from exponential worst-case complexity. The slide concludes by suggesting that the inherent "myopia" of the simplex method makes it susceptible to such worst-case scenarios, regardless of the specific pivoting rule used.  The notation $2^n - 1$ refers to the number of iterations required by the largest-coefficient rule in the Klee-Minty problem with $n$ variables. The variables $m$ and $n$ likely represent the number of constraints and variables, respectively, in the linear program. The context of linear programming is crucial for understanding the discussion of pivoting rules and their impact on the efficiency of the simplex method.

Table 4.2 similarly presents data for the largest-increase rule. 8.latex:
\textbf{Other Pivoting Rules (independent of scale)} \\
Which of the two rules is better? On problems arising from applications, the \\
number of iterations required by the largest increase is \underline{usually} smaller than the \\
number of iterations required by the largest coefficient. Simulation experiments lead \\
to a similar outcome (see Table 4.2). \\
Nevertheless, as the largest-coefficient rule takes less time to execute than the \\
largest increase, it is the \underline{former} that usually wins in terms of total computing time. \\
More generally, the number of iterations is a poor criterion for assessing the effi- \\
ciency of a rule for choosing the entering variable. It is the total computing time that \\
counts, and rules that tend to reduce the number of iterations often take too much \\
time to execute. In this light, even the largest-coefficient rule is found too time- \\
consuming and therefore rarely, if ever, used in practice. The choice of entering \\
variables in efficient implementations of the simplex method is influenced by the \\
logistics of handling large problems on a computer; this matter will be studied in \\
Chapter 7.

\end{itemize}

\textbf{Spanning Trees and Bases} \\
The above computation suggests that spanning trees are related to bases in the simplex method. Let us pursue this idea. Normally, a basis is an invertible square submatrix of the constraint matrix. But for incidence matrices, no such submatrix exists. To see why, note that if we sum together all the rows of A, we get a row vector of all zeros (since each column of A has exactly one +1 and one -1). Of course, every square submatrix of A has this same property and so is singular. In fact, we shall show in a moment that for a connected network, there is exactly one redundant equation (i.e., the rank of A is exactly $m - 1$). \\
Let us select some node, say, the last one, and delete the flow balance constraint associated with this node from the constraints defining the problem (since it is redundant anyway). Let us call this node the root node. Let $\tilde{A}$ denote the incidence matrix A without the row corresponding to the root node (i.e., the last row), and let $\tilde{b}$ denote the supply/demand vector with the last entry deleted. The most important property of network flow problems is summarized in the following theorem: \\
\textbf{THEOREM 14.1.} A square submatrix of $\tilde{A}$ is a basis if and only if the arcs to which its columns correspond form a spanning tree.

The key reason is that summing all rows of the incidence matrix A always results in a zero vector, implying singularity of any square submatrix.  The slide then introduces a modified approach: selecting a root node, deleting the corresponding row from the incidence matrix A (resulting in $\tilde{A}$), and deleting the corresponding entry from the supply/demand vector $b$ (resulting in $\tilde{b}$).  Finally, Theorem 14.1 is presented, stating that a square submatrix of $\tilde{A}$ forms a basis if and only if the corresponding arcs in the network constitute a spanning tree. This theorem establishes a fundamental connection between the linear algebra of the problem (bases) and the graph theory of the network (spanning trees).

23.description:
Slide 23 of 45 in a Linear Programming course describes the update rules for dual variables and dual slacks in the Primal Network Simplex algorithm.  The slide is divided into two sections: "Dual variables update" and "Dual slacks update".

The "Dual variables update" section outlines two cases:

1. If the entering arc connects the root-containing tree to a non-root-containing tree, then all dual variables in the non-root-containing tree are increased by the dual slack of the entering arc.
2. Otherwise (if the entering arc connects nodes within the same tree), these dual variables are decreased by the dual slack of the entering arc.

The "Dual slacks update" section explains how the dual slacks of the arcs are updated:

Dual slacks corresponding to arcs bridging in the same direction as the entering arc are decremented by the old dual slack on the entering arc.  Dual slacks corresponding to arcs bridging in the opposite direction are incremented by the old dual slack on the entering arc.

The context of Linear Programming is crucial here, as these update rules are specific to the network simplex method used to solve linear programs represented as networks.  The terms "dual variables," "dual slacks," "root-containing tree," and "non-root-containing tree" are all standard terminology within network optimization algorithms.  The slide provides a concise summary of the update rules, crucial for implementing the Primal Network Simplex algorithm.

\underline{\text{Dual Network Simplex}} \\
\text{To this end, let us consider the general situation. As mentioned above, the spanning} \\
\text{tree with the leaving arc removed consists of two disjoint trees. The entering arc must} \\
\text{reconnect these two trees.} \\
\text{First, consider a reconnecting arc that connects in the same direction as the leaving} \\
\text{arc. If chosen as the entering arc, this arc will become basic in which case its dual} \\
\text{slack will drop from a positive value to zero. The dual slack for all other nontree arcs} \\
\text{pointing in the same direction will drop by the same amount. The leaving arc will} \\
\text{become a nontree arc and therefore its dual slack will also drop by this amount. But, it} \\
\text{\underline{started out at zero}. After the pivot, it will be negative. In other words, dual feasibility} \\
\text{will be lost. For this reason, we restrict our attention to reconnecting arcs that point in} \\
\text{\underline{the opposite direction}.} \\
\text{\textbf{Entering arc selection rule:}} \\
\text{$\bullet$ the entering arc must bridge the two subtrees in the \underline{opposite}} \\
\text{direction from the leaving arc, and} \\
\text{$\bullet$ among all such arcs, it must have the \underline{smallest dual slack}.}

45.latex:
\underline{\text{5. Putting It All Together}}

As we saw in Chapter 5, for linear programming the primal and the dual simplex methods form the foundation on which one can build a few different variants of the simplex method. The same is true here in the context of network flows.

For example, one can build a two-phased procedure in which one first uses the dual network simplex method (with costs artificially and temporarily altered to ensure dual feasibility of an initial tree solution) to find a primal feasible solution and then uses the primal network simplex method to move from the feasible solution to an optimal one.

Alternatively, one can use the primal network simplex method (with supplies temporarily altered to ensure primal feasibility of an initial tree solution) to find a dual feasible solution and then use the dual network simplex method (with the original supplies) to move from the dual feasible solution to an optimal one.

Finally, as described for linear programming in Chapter 7, one can define a parametric self-dual method in which primal pivots and dual pivots are intermingled as needed so as to reduce a perturbation parameter $\mu$ from $\infty$ to zero.

Each strategy involves modifying the problem's parameters (costs or supplies) to ensure feasibility before applying the appropriate simplex method.  The mention of Chapter 5 and Chapter 7 indicates that these chapters covered the foundational simplex methods and the parametric self-dual method, respectively. 11.description: Slide 11 of 24 in a Linear Programming course states the Strong Duality Theorem.  The theorem asserts that if a primal linear programming problem (P) has an optimal solution $x_j^*$, then its corresponding dual problem (D) also has an optimal solution $y_i^*$.  Furthermore, the optimal objective function values of both problems are equal; that is, $\sum_j c_j x_j^* = \sum_i b_i y_i^* = \zeta^*$, where $\zeta^*$ represents the optimal objective function value. This equality is also referred to as the duality gap being zero. The slide notes that the proof of the theorem provides a method for calculating the optimal dual solution $y_i^*$ given the optimal primal solution $x_j^*$. The context of the course is crucial for understanding the relationship between primal and dual linear programming problems and the implications of strong duality for solving these problems efficiently.

18.description:
Slide 18 of 24 in a Linear Programming course outlines four possible scenarios regarding the solutions of a primal linear program (P) and its corresponding dual linear program (D).  The slide is titled "Four and Only Four Possibilities".

The first scenario (\textcircled{1}) states that if (P) has an optimal solution, then (D) also has an optimal solution, and the optimal objective function values of both problems are equal ($\zeta^* = \xi^*$), resulting in a zero duality gap.

The second scenario (\textcircled{2}) states that if (P) is feasible but unbounded (meaning its objective function can be made arbitrarily large), then (D) must be infeasible (meaning it has no feasible solution).  This is because the weak duality theorem ($\zeta(x) \le \xi(y)$ for all feasible $x$ and $y$) implies that if $\zeta(x)$ can be arbitrarily large, then $\xi(y)$ must be unbounded above, which is impossible for a feasible dual problem.  The notation $\zeta^* = \xi^* = +\infty$ indicates that both objective functions tend to infinity, and the parenthetical comment clarifies that the minimum of an empty set is conventionally defined as $+\infty$.  The arrows indicate the implications between the primal and dual problem's solution status. The context of the course is crucial for understanding the relationship between primal and dual linear programs and the implications of their feasibility and boundedness.

23.description: Slide 23 of 24 in a Linear Programming course shows a proof of complementary slackness. The proof starts with the equation $\sum_j c_j x_j = \sum_j \left( \sum_i a_{ij} y_i \right) x_j$, which is a consequence of primal and dual feasibility and strong duality.  The circled "1" likely indicates a step or assumption from a previous slide or part of the proof.  Subtracting the left side from the right side yields $0 = \sum_j \left( \sum_i a_{ij} y_i - c_j \right) x_j$. The expression $\sum_i a_{ij} y_i - c_j$ is identified as the dual slack variable $z_j$. This leads to the equation $0 = \sum_j z_j x_j$. Since both $z_j$ and $x_j$ are non-negative, the only way for their sum to be zero is if each term $z_j x_j = 0$ for all $j$. This is the complementary slackness condition. The implication arrow ($\implies$) indicates the conclusion of the proof. The context of the course is crucial for understanding the mathematical manipulations and the significance of complementary slackness in linear programming optimization.

5.description: Slide 5 of 7 in a Linear Programming course demonstrates weak duality.  The slide starts by assuming $\hat{x}$ is a feasible solution to the primal problem (P).  It then defines $\xi(\hat{x}) = c^T \hat{x}$ and manipulates this expression using the constraints of the primal problem ($Ax \le b$ and $x \le u$) and the non-negativity of the dual variables $y$ and $z$.  The inequalities $y \ge 0$, $Ax - b \le 0$, $z \ge 0$, and $x - u \le 0$ are used to show that $\xi(\hat{x})$ is less than or equal to the expression $\max_x (c^T x - y^T (Ax - b) - z^T (x - u))$. This maximum is then defined as $\xi(y, z)$. The core concept of weak duality is then stated: $\xi(\hat{x}) \le \xi(y, z)$, meaning the objective function value of any feasible solution to the primal problem is less than or equal to the objective function value of any feasible solution to the dual problem.  The implication is shown: if $x$ is a feasible solution to the primal problem, then the maximum value of the primal objective function ($\xi^*$) is less than or equal to the minimum value of the dual objective function ($\xi^*$). The red arrows indicate the direction of the inequalities and implications. The context of the course is crucial for understanding the relationship between the primal and dual problems and the significance of weak duality in optimization.

17.description: Slide 17 of 21 in a Linear Programming course introduces Bellman's equation for solving the shortest path problem.  A simple directed acyclic graph is shown, with nodes $i$ (source), $j$, $k$, $l$, and $r$ (destination).  The edge from node $i$ to node $j$ has a weight $c_{ij}$.  The nodes $i$ and $j$ are labeled with $V_i$ and $V_j$ respectively, representing the shortest distance from that node to the destination node $r$. Bellman's equation, $V_i = \min_j \{c_{ij} + V_j\}$, is presented in a box. This equation recursively defines the shortest distance from node $i$ to the destination node $r$ as the minimum of the sum of the weight of the edge from $i$ to $j$ and the shortest distance from $j$ to $r$, considering all possible neighboring nodes $j$. The equation $V_r = 0$ indicates that the shortest distance from the destination node $r$ to itself is 0. The context of the course (Linear Programming) is important because dynamic programming techniques, such as Bellman's equation, are used to solve optimization problems, including shortest path problems, which can be formulated as linear programs.

15.description: Slide 15 of 17 in a Linear Programming course presents the linear programming (LP) formulation of the Max Flow Min Cut problem.  The objective function is to minimize $-x_{ts}$, where $x_{ts}$ represents the flow on a fictitious arc from the sink to the source.  Minimizing $-x_{ts}$ is equivalent to maximizing $x_{ts}$, which represents the total flow through the network. The constraints ensure flow conservation at each node: the total flow entering a node equals the total flow leaving the node.  The summation notation $\sum_j x_{sj}$ represents the total flow leaving the source node, and $\sum_i x_{it}$ represents the total flow entering the sink node. The constraint $\sum_i x_{ik} = \sum_j x_{kj}$ for $k \ne s, t$ enforces flow conservation at all intermediate nodes. The inequalities $0 \le x_{ij} \le u_{ij}$ represent the capacity constraints on each arc $(i,j)$, where $u_{ij}$ is the capacity of the arc. The capacity of the fictitious arc from the sink to the source is assumed to be infinite ($u_{ts} = +\infty$). This LP formulation provides a way to solve the maximum flow problem using linear programming techniques. The context of linear programming is crucial because this slide shows how a network flow problem can be transformed into an equivalent linear program, which can then be solved using standard LP algorithms.

The figure illustrates a key step in the proof: handling upper bounds on arc capacities.  The top part of the figure shows a single arc $(i,j)$ with capacity $u_{ij}$ and flow $x_{ij}$. The bottom part shows the same arc decomposed by introducing a new node $k$, splitting the arc into two arcs: $(i,k)$ with capacity $u_{ij}$ and flow $x_{ij}$, and $(k,j)$ with infinite capacity and flow $t_{ij}$. These conditions relate the flow ($x_{ij}$) on an arc to the dual variables ($y_i$, $y_j$) and the cost ($c_{ij}$) associated with that arc.  The conditions are based on whether the flow is zero, at capacity, or strictly between zero and capacity. The final equation, $x_{ij} + t_{ij} = u_{ij}$, explicitly shows how the introduction of the new node $k$ allows the handling of the upper bound $u_{ij}$ on the flow. The context of linear programming is crucial because this slide demonstrates a proof technique that leverages the duality theory of linear programming to prove a fundamental theorem in network flow optimization.

\text{Proof of Max Flow = Min Cut (LP)} \\
\text{Let } x_{ij}^*, (i, j) \in A, \text{ denote the optimal values of the primal variables, and let } y_i^*, \\ i \in N, \text{ denote the optimal values of the dual variables. Then the complementarity} \\ \text{conditions (15.6) imply that} \\
(15.9) \quad x_{ij}^* = 0 \quad \text{whenever } y_i^* + c_{ij} > y_j^* \\
(15.10) \quad x_{ij}^* = u_{ij} \quad \text{whenever } y_i^* + c_{ij} < y_j^* \\
\text{In particular,} \\
y_i^* - 1 \ge y_s^* \\
(\text{since } u_{ts} = \infty). \text{ Put } C^* = \{k : y_k^* \le y_s^*\}. \text{ Clearly, } C^* \text{ is a cut.} \\
\text{Consider an arc having its tail in } C^* \text{ and its head in the complement of } C^*. \text{ It} \\ \text{follows from the definition of } C^* \text{ that } y_i^* \le y_s^* < y_j^*. \text{ Since } c_{ij} \text{ is zero, we see} \\ \text{from (15.10) that } x_{ij}^* = u_{ij}. \\
\text{Now consider an original arc having its tail in the complement of } C^* \text{ and its head} \\ \text{in } C^* \text{ (i.e., bridging the two sets in the opposite direction). It follows then that } y_j^* \le \\ y_s^* < y_i^*. \text{ Hence, we see from (15.9) that } x_{ij}^* = 0.

figures.description: Handwritten proof of the Max Flow Min Cut theorem using linear programming duality. The proof uses complementarity conditions (15.9) and (15.10) derived from the linear program and its dual.  A cut $C^*$ is defined based on the dual variables $y_i^*$. The proof then analyzes arcs with tails and heads in $C^*$ and its complement to show that the maximum flow equals the minimum cut.

17.description: Slide 17 of 17 in a Linear Programming course completes the proof of the Max Flow Min Cut theorem using linear programming duality. The proof starts by stating the complementarity conditions (15.9) and (15.10) which relate the optimal primal variables ($x_{ij}^*$ representing flow) and dual variables ($y_i^*$) of the linear programming formulation of the max-flow problem.  A cut $C^*$ is defined as the set of nodes $k$ such that $y_k^* \le y_s^*$, where $s$ is the source node. The proof then considers two cases: arcs with tails in $C^*$ and heads outside $C^*$, and arcs with tails outside $C^*$ and heads in $C^*$. By applying the complementarity conditions (15.9) and (15.10) and the definition of the cut $C^*$, the proof shows that the flow on arcs crossing the cut $C^*$ in one direction is at capacity, while the flow on arcs crossing in the opposite direction is zero. This directly implies that the maximum flow equals the capacity of the minimum cut, thus proving the Max Flow Min Cut theorem. The context of linear programming is crucial because this slide demonstrates a proof technique that leverages the duality theory of linear programming to prove a fundamental theorem in network flow optimization.  The notation $u_{ij}$ represents the capacity of arc $(i,j)$, and $c_{ij}$ represents the cost associated with that arc (likely 0 in this context).

4.description: Slide 4 of 22 presents the least squares regression problem in the context of a linear programming course.  The slide begins by defining the problem as minimizing the sum of squared errors: $\min_{(x_1, \dots, x_n)} \sum_i \left[ \left( b_i - \sum_j a_{ij} x_j \right)^2 \right]$, where $b_i$ represents the observed values, $a_{ij}$ represents the attributes, and $x_j$ are the parameters to be estimated. This is equivalently expressed in matrix notation as $\min_X ||b - AX||_2^2$, where $b$ is a vector of observed values, $A$ is a matrix of attributes, and $X$ is a vector of parameters. The slide then shows that the system of equations $AX = b$ might not be solvable, leading to the derivation of the normal equation $A^T A \hat{X} = A^T b$, which always has a solution if the matrix $A^T A$ is invertible.  The solution is then given as $\hat{X} = (A^T A)^{-1} A^T b$, provided that the inverse exists. The parenthetical comments highlight the solvability conditions. The context of linear programming is relevant because the least squares problem can be formulated as a quadratic programming problem, a close relative of linear programming.  The slide lays the groundwork for later discussions on how linear programming techniques can be applied to solve or approximate solutions to least squares problems, especially in cases where the matrix $A^T A$ is not invertible or ill-conditioned.

5.description: Slide 5 of 22 introduces L1 regression, a type of regression analysis that minimizes the sum of the absolute differences between the observed and predicted values.  The slide first presents the problem as minimizing the L1 norm of the residual vector: $\min_X ||b - AX||_1$, where $b$ is the vector of observed values, $A$ is the matrix of attributes, and $X$ is the vector of parameters to be estimated.  This is equivalent to minimizing the sum of absolute errors: $\min_{(x_1, \dots, x_n)} \sum_i |b_i - \sum_j a_{ij} x_j|$.  The slide then shows how this problem can be reformulated as a linear program by introducing slack variables $t_i$ for each data point. The objective function becomes $\min_i \sum_{i=1}^m t_i$, and the constraints are $-t_i \le b_i - \sum_j a_{ij} x_j \le t_i$, which ensures that each $t_i$ is greater than or equal to the absolute error $|b_i - \sum_j a_{ij} x_j|$.  This reformulation is crucial because it allows the use of linear programming techniques to solve the L1 regression problem. The arrow points to the constraint that is derived from the absolute value. The context of the course (Linear Programming) is essential here, as the slide demonstrates how a seemingly non-linear problem (L1 regression) can be transformed into a linear program, making it solvable using linear programming algorithms.

2.description: Slide 2 of 22 introduces the Lagrangian method for solving linear programming problems with equality constraints. The top box shows a primal problem where the objective is to maximize $f_0(x)$ subject to $n$ equality constraints $g_j(x) = 0$.  The red arrow points to $\mathcal{C}$, likely representing the constraint set. The bottom box introduces the Lagrangian function $L(x, \mu) = f_0(x) - \sum_{j=1}^n \mu_j g_j(x)$, where $\mu_j$ are the Lagrange multipliers.  Maximizing this Lagrangian function is equivalent to the original constrained problem, but without explicit constraints. The red arrow points to "no constraints" to emphasize this point. The slide explains how to transform a constrained optimization problem into an unconstrained one using the method of Lagrange multipliers. This is a crucial step in solving linear programming problems, especially when dealing with equality constraints. The context of linear programming is essential to understand the significance of the Lagrangian method in finding optimal solutions.

The equivalence $-x \le 0$ is also shown, highlighting the transformation of the non-negativity constraint into a standard inequality form. The slide then introduces the Lagrangian $L(x, y, \lambda) = c^T x - y^T(Ax - b) - \lambda^T(-x)$, where $y$ and $\lambda$ are the Lagrange multipliers associated with the inequality constraints $Ax \le b$ and $x \ge 0$, respectively. The non-negativity constraints $y \ge 0$ and $\lambda \ge 0$ are explicitly stated. The Lagrangian is then simplified to $L(x, y, \lambda) = (c^T - y^T A + \lambda^T)x + y^T b$. This sets the stage for deriving the dual problem in subsequent slides. The boxed equation highlights the primal problem formulation.

2.description: Slide 2 of 23 discusses integer programming and the limitations of a naive approach to solving it. The slide begins by formally defining an integer programming problem: maximize $\xi(x) = c^T x$ subject to $Ax \le b$, $x \ge 0$, and $x_j \in \mathbb{Z}$ for all $j$.  The notation is standard for linear programming, with $c$ representing the objective function coefficients, $A$ the constraint matrix, $b$ the constraint vector, and $x$ the vector of decision variables. The crucial difference from linear programming is the integrality constraint $x_j \in \mathbb{Z}$, indicating that the variables must take integer values. The slide then explains why simply solving the relaxed problem (ignoring the integrality constraints) and rounding the solution is not a reliable method. Two reasons are given: (1) the rounded solution might not be feasible (i.e., it might violate the constraints $Ax \le b$), and (2) the optimal integer solution might be far from the rounded solution, leading to a suboptimal result. The term "relaxed problem" refers to the linear programming problem obtained by removing the integrality constraints. The context of the course (Linear Programming) is essential because this slide highlights the key differences and challenges of integer programming compared to its linear counterpart.

11.description: Slide 11 of 23 discusses the advantages of depth-first search over breadth-first search in the branch-and-bound algorithm for integer programming problems.  The slide begins by stating that a depth-first search ("going deep before going wide") is generally preferred. Three reasons are given. The first reason is that most integer solutions are found deep within the enumeration tree.  Two advantages of finding a feasible integer solution early are then explained. First, it allows for early termination of the search if a satisfactory solution is found. Second, and more importantly, finding a feasible integer solution allows for "pruning" the tree.  This pruning occurs because any node with an objective function value worse than the best feasible integer solution found so far can be eliminated from further consideration, significantly improving efficiency. The highlighted terms "integer solutions" and "feasible solution" emphasize the core concept of finding integer solutions within the feasible region of the problem. The context of linear programming is crucial because this slide explains a key algorithmic optimization technique used to solve integer programming problems, a common extension of linear programming.
